boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Piedmont record (June 5-6, 1864) in the Lynchburg Campaign [May-June 1864]. The frozen interval includes the occupation of Staunton on June 6. Hunter's May 26-June 4 advance, the June 4 flank march by Port Republic and the June 8 junction with Crook and Averell are context. Campaign marches, the destruction at Staunton and Lexington, the retreat to the Kanawha and campaign-wide loss and capture totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force text and side rows give 14,000 total (US 8,500; CS 5,500), and the live page repeats them. Pond says Hunter left Cedar Creek on May 26 with 8,500 men of all arms and twenty-one guns. Hunter says papers on Jones's body put the Confederate force at between 6,000 and 7,000 men and 16 guns. Vaughn reported that he went into the fight with an aggregate of 5,600 and had not over 3,000 effectives the next day, including 800 of Imboden's cavalry (Pond quotes this dispatch with 'effectives' for 'effective men'); he put Hunter at not less than 9,000 or 10,000 infantry with heavy cavalry and thirty guns, and the next day at about 10,000 men and twenty-four guns. An inspection report abstracted in Pond's appendix says Smith's brigade fought at Piedmont with dismounted cavalry and the Forty-fifth regiment.
claims.rationale: Pond's 8,500 is Hunter's strength at the start of the march, not on June 5. Vaughn's 5,600 is an aggregate on the day and his 3,000 an after-battle effective count; Hunter's 6,000-7,000 comes from captured papers. The frozen 8,500 matches Pond's starting figure and the frozen 5,500 is near Vaughn's 5,600, but their basis is not established. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Hunter found the enemy 'advan¬ tageously posted' at Piedmont, seven miles southwest of Port Republic, with an advanced position in a wood behind defenses of fallen timber and fence rails; Pond puts the main works on a curving range of thickly timbered hills. Thoburn took elevated ground on the Union left and crossed the open valley (Pond: a ravine) to strike the flank, and part of the Confederate force was driven over the steep bank into the river covering its left.
claims.rationale: Hills, ravine and river predate the battle; the fallen-timber and rail defenses were Confederate field works of unstated age, so the claim is not tagged inherited. No map verification.

claims.value: Hunter says he spent June 3 ascertaining the enemy's force and position at Mount Crawford and then moved by a side road so little expected that he surprised a supply train; his advanced cavalry met the enemy's at 6 a.m. on the 5th. His figure for Jones's strength came from papers found on Jones's body after the battle. Vaughn's estimates of Hunter's strength varied from 9,000-10,000 infantry with heavy cavalry to about 10,000 men.
claims.rationale: Hunter's surprise statement is his inference; the papers were read after the battle.

claims.value: The frozen and live commanders are Major General David Hunter (US) and Brigadier General William E. Jones (CS). Hunter reports Moor's first attack failing at 1 p.m. and then sending orders for Thoburn's brigade to cross the valley and strike the enemy's flank, which proved decisive, with Moor and Wynkoop's cavalry joining; NPS credits the flanking movement to Thoburn's brigade. Jones was killed on the field (Hunter, Vaughn), and the command devolved on Vaughn, who fell back toward Waynesborough. Pond says Stahel was wounded leading his command.
claims.rationale: Hunter ordered the flank attack; Thoburn executed it. Jones's command ended with his death during the battle, so the retreat was Vaughn's. No listed commander receives automatic credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results are Union victory. Hunter says the enemy fled in confusion and that he occupied Staunton without opposition on June 6; Vaughn reported that he had been driven back, retired to Fishersville with his command much scattered, and feared he would be forced to leave the Valley; Pond says the enemy abandoned the entire position.
claims.rationale: The accounts agree on the tactical result. The destruction at Staunton and the junction with Crook are campaign context.

claims.value: The frozen totals are 2,375 (US 875; CS 1500), with the same side values in the force rows; the live page gives 2,475 (US 875; CS 1,600) and says more than 1,000 Confederates, including 60 officers, were captured and three guns lost. Hunter reports over 1,000 prisoners including 60 officers, Confederate killed and wounded estimated at 600 and as many again lost by straggling, 400 sick and wounded captured at Staunton, and his own loss through June 8 as under 500 killed and wounded. Pond gives over a thousand captured on the field, about 1,500 prisoners in all, three guns, and a Union loss of 420. Vaughn reported 60 wounded left on the field, the enemy's killed and wounded at 1,500, and 1,000 prisoners taken.
claims.rationale: Hunter's under 500 covers operations through June 8; Pond's 1,500 prisoners adds the Staunton sick and wounded; Vaughn's 1,500 is his estimate of Union losses. None is reconciled. Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Ely's and Campbell's reports on Piedmont (Nos. 4-5), E. G. Lee's reports (No. 24) and the compiled composition-and-losses table (No. 2, which covers June 10-23 and was read, not selected) remain deferred; no Imboden report on Piedmont was located in the inspected report list. Bragg's June 6 covering letter to the Secretary of War was read and not selected.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office; in these chapters it quotes Sigel's, Hunter's, Vaughn's and Imboden's reports and despatches and Strother's report, so it is not independent of those families. Hunter's June 8 report and Vaughn's June 5-7 dispatches (the targeted follow-up, for the Confederate account after Jones's death) printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVII, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
